author: James De La Fuente
title: Animal shelters fear closure amid new regulations - NewsBreak
text:
By James De La Fuente ,
1 hours ago
CAPITAL REGION, N.Y. ( NEWS10 ) — As some Capital Region leaders are calling the outbreak in animal abuse cases an epidemic, tough new regulatory standards for animal shelters will go into effect December 15 th of this year. Some of the local animal shelters and rescues in the area said they are worried the changes could shut them down.
Get the latest news, weather, sports and entertainment delivered right to your inbox! “We knew right away that our current facility would not meet the new requirements of this law.” Lynette Koch with Whiskers Animal Benevolent League said the new regulations regarding capacity limits, spacing of animals, temperature control and vet care, are very costly. “Between purchasing the building and renovating, it would likely be between $3 million and $4 million.”
The leadership at the Mohawk Hudson Humane Society explained they too are dealing with the adjustments. “I will tell you, as of right now, we are still not 100% in compliance. If we lose power for more than 4 hours, we have a plan to either evacuate the animals or have backup source of energy that would cost us about $110,000 to get a new generator in here,” said CEO Ashley Jeffrey Bouck.
Officials call for regulations, oversight of NY animal boarders The CEO went on to explain that she’s concerned that the smaller operations will struggle the most, “For the those of us who have been working very hard to provide, you know, a gold standard of care, all the must areas for the ASV (Association of Shelter Veterinarians) guidelines, some of them may unintentionally be closed down because of this.”
Libby Post is the New York State Animal Protection Federation ’s Executive Director, and she spearheaded the new regulations and said folks need not be afraid. “No one’s getting shut down. And ultimately what AG and markets wants to see is progress,” said Post.
Post explained that the regulations needed to be upgraded to bring shelters and rescues to a same standard, “It’s recordkeeping, it’s training, physical plant, veterinary care, husbandry, foster care, transport. It covers everything that needs to be covered.”
She also said there is help available for those who are struggling with the new requirements, “We have over the last three years raised close to a half a million dollars in grant funding to provide no cost consulting services .”
